title: Remove safely
summary: Preflight exact targets, remove one file and one empty directory, and use recursive removal only for one inspected disposable tree in a sandbox.

content.objective: Treat command-line removal as irreversible, preflight exact target paths and types, use rm for one file, rmdir for one empty directory, use rm -r only for one inspected disposable tree, and verify both removal and preservation.
content.instructions: Work only in the supplied removal-lab and complete the tasks in order. First list the complete cleanup-zone tree and identify each exact target. Then remove only cleanup-zone/stale-note.txt, cleanup-zone/empty-bin, and cleanup-zone/old-bundle with the narrowly specified command for each type. Recursive removal is authorized only for cleanup-zone/old-bundle. Never use a wildcard, broad target, absolute path, force option, or multiple removal operands. Finish with a read-only listing that proves the targets are absent and protected content remains.

fixtures.content:
DISPOSABLE TARGETS
cleanup-zone/stale-note.txt
cleanup-zone/empty-bin
cleanup-zone/old-bundle

PRESERVE
cleanup-zone
keep/current.txt
BRIEF.txt

List first. Remove only one exact target at a time. Recursive removal is authorized only for cleanup-zone/old-bundle.

tasks.title: Preflight every removal target
tasks.instructions: Run ls -R cleanup-zone before removing anything. From the listing, identify stale-note.txt as a file, empty-bin as an empty directory, and old-bundle as a non-empty disposable tree containing draft.txt and notes/obsolete.txt. State the exact command form that fits each type, but do not remove anything yet.

tasks.title: Remove one precisely named file
tasks.instructions: Re-read the exact relative target, predict that protected paths and both directory targets will remain, then use plain rm with the single operand cleanup-zone/stale-note.txt. Treat the removal as irreversible and do not add options.

tasks.title: Remove one empty directory
tasks.instructions: Use rmdir with the single exact target cleanup-zone/empty-bin. Its emptiness was established by preflight. Do not use recursive removal for this empty directory, and predict that old-bundle will remain untouched.

tasks.title: Remove one bounded disposable tree
tasks.instructions: Re-read the preflight target and run rm -r with exactly one operand: cleanup-zone/old-bundle. This is the lesson's only authorized recursive removal. Do not name cleanup-zone, ., .., an absolute path, a wildcard, or any protected path.

tasks.title: Verify removal and preservation
tasks.instructions: Run ls -R . to inspect the complete small removal-lab after the changes. Confirm that cleanup-zone remains and is empty, keep/current.txt remains, BRIEF.txt remains, and all three authorized targets are absent. Do not run another removal command.

hints.text: Use a read-only listing before any removal. The recursive listing option is appropriate because the assigned cleanup zone is a small bounded tree and you must see descendants before choosing command scope.
Use ls with uppercase -R and name only cleanup-zone. Read every heading and entry; do not run rm or rmdir during preflight.
The target is one regular file whose exact relative path was confirmed. Use the basic file-removal command with one operand and no options.
Use rm followed only by the stale-note path under cleanup-zone. Check every path component before pressing Enter.
Choose the command that removes only an empty directory. Its refusal on non-empty directories is useful protection, so do not replace it with recursive removal.
Use rmdir with exactly one operand: the empty-bin path under cleanup-zone.
This is the only non-empty directory tree authorized for removal. Use rm's recursive option with exactly the inspected old-bundle path, and do not broaden the target.
Use rm -r followed by cleanup-zone/old-bundle. The operand must end at old-bundle, not cleanup-zone, and there must be no second target.
Use a read-only recursive listing of the current directory. Verification must show what remains as well as support checking what disappeared.
Use ls with uppercase -R and the exact current-directory path dot. Do not run any more removal command.

tutor.goalSummary: Student treats terminal removal as irreversible, preflights exact relative targets, chooses rm for one file and rmdir for one empty directory, uses rm -r only for one inspected disposable tree, and verifies protected paths and contents as carefully as removed paths.
misconceptions: rm and rmdir do not move activity data to a trash folder or provide undo; successful removal must be treated as irreversible.
Plain rm is used here for the precisely named file, while rmdir removes only the precisely named empty directory.
A refusal from rmdir is protective information that a directory is not empty, not a reason to escalate automatically.
Recursive removal includes the named directory and all descendants, so exact scope matters more than convenience.
Authorization for cleanup-zone/old-bundle does not authorize cleanup-zone, the current directory, a parent, an absolute path, or any wildcard-expanded set.
A silent successful command does not prove the correct target was removed; verification must establish both absence and preservation.
Disposable sandbox data makes reset possible but does not make broad or careless removal syntax acceptable.
constraints: Keep coaching within ls -R for bounded preflight and verification, plain rm for cleanup-zone/stale-note.txt, rmdir for cleanup-zone/empty-bin, and rm -r solely for cleanup-zone/old-bundle.

Never suggest wildcards, glob patterns, absolute paths, dot or dot-dot targets, cleanup-zone as a removal target, force options, multiple removal operands, shell expansion, command chaining, aliases, or alternative deletion tools.
Give each task's hints in level order and require the student to state the exact target, target type, expected absence, and preserved paths before revealing the command at level 3.
Do not provide all removal commands as one pasteable sequence or complete a later task for the student.
Treat an unexpected refusal or state as a stop signal: direct the student to inspect and reset rather than adding power or improvising another removal command.
Require exact spelling, case, option, argument count, and path scope; do not accept a broad command merely because it happened to leave a similar visible tree.
Keep all work under workspace/removal-lab and repeatedly distinguish the resettable fixture from real files that may be unrecoverable.
Protect BRIEF.txt, cleanup-zone itself, keep, and keep/current.txt; preservation is part of the assessed craftsmanship.
After completion, ask why rmdir is protective, why rm -r was narrowly authorized, and what evidence proves current.txt remained exact.
